newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - USAir gets new name, but faces old issues.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - USAir gets new name, but faces old issues.

text.p: USAir Group Inc on Tuesday unveiled plans for a new name and livery design, but beneath the new paint remains an airline still burdened with old problems of high costs and growing competition.
USAir offered no new "strategy change, but showed that they are executing it better," said Glenn Engel, an analyst with Goldman Sachs.
Early next year, USAir will change its name to US Airways to "signal the change in scope and size of the airline," USAir's executive vice president of marketing W.T. Lagow said.
USAir said the new name reflects its goals to expand independently and internationally, instead of merging with a rival carrier.

"It's a cosmetic change, but it would certainly indicate that they're going to make a go of it independently. They're not likely to change the livery if they're going to turn around and sell it quickly," said Brian Harris, an airline analyst with Lehman Brothers.
USAir and UAL Corp were once considered merger candidates, but USAir Chairman Stephen Wolf said the carrier is not in merger talks and sees none on the horizon.
"Our preference has been for internally-generated growth and that remains our preferred course of action," Wolf said.
USAir said it sees "fast, big growth" in its international operations and plans to add up to 23 new international markets from Philadelphia and other key cities within the "next few years."
"We have inherent, fundamental strength to Europe that needs to be exploited," USAir president Rakesh Gangwal said.
In 1997, USAir said it expects domestic growth of about 0.7 percent and total system growth of about 2.0 percent.
USAir, which recently said it will end its code-sharing relationship with British Airways Plc in March 1997, said it expects to eventually pursue other international alliances.
"Long-term we want to participate with somebody, but it's not real high on our radar scope at this time," Wolf said.
But USAir faces some difficult problems at home, such as a high cost structure and growing competition from low-cost carriers such as Southwest Airlines Co and Delta Air Lines's Express unit.
"We have to compete with the likes of Southwest. We have a need for a low-cost response" or a no-frills product with low employee costs and low distribution expenses, Gangwal said.
The airline declined to comment on what form the low-cost "solution" may take, but management and labor are discussing various possibilities.
Wolf, however, said he expect's USAir's low-cost plan to affect a larger percentage of the company than seen with Delta Express or the Shuttle by United, part of UAL Corp.
USAir and its labor groups also are in talks to reduce operating costs, which remain among the highest in the industry. Labor costs comprise about 40 percent of USAir's operating costs.
USAir said its recent order for up to 400 Airbus Industrie structure."
"The company needs fixing. That's very obvious. Our employee costs are very high," Gangwal said.
USAir's hope to get a new cost structure in time to secure financing for its first Airbus jets in 1997 is "an obvious carrot for the unions," Harris said.
Although USAir can cancel the Airbus order without penalty, analysts expect the carrier to eventually secure financing for the deal.
